title: Ancient meteorite holds clues to Mars' watery past
excerpt: A meteorite discovered in Mali is one of the oldest pieces of Mars ever found on Earth. Its minerals hold evidence of water interacting with the planet’s crust more than 4 billion years ago.
content:
A meteorite discovered in Mali is one of the oldest pieces of Mars ever found on Earth. Its minerals hold evidence of water interacting with the planet’s crust more than 4 billion years ago.

Posted 10/29/2026, 10:06:52 PM

By Tony Rice, NASA Ambassador

M — A rose-colored rock weighing less than 2 pounds discovered in the Sahara Desert the abandoned salt mines northern Mali, a land locked country in western Africa revealed a remarkable history that began more than 4.1 billion years ago, when Mars was still in its earliest stages of development.

A study published Thursday in the journal Science describes how researchers determined the meteorite’s age and identified evidence of ancient interactions between water and rock. The findings make Teghaza 001 one of the three oldest Martian meteorites known on Earth and offer scientists a rare opportunity to study material from the Red Planet’s ancient crust.

Other WRAL Top Stories

A journey from Mars to Earth

The meteorite, named Teghaza 001, began its history deep in the geological past of Mars. Its volcanic minerals formed as magma cooled and crystallized, creating rock that became part of the planet’s crust. Later, water changed the rock, leaving behind chemical and mineralogical clues about conditions on early Mars.

Scientists believe the meteorite may have originated in the planet’s southern highlands, an ancient, heavily cratered region. Researchers identified 13 locations on Mars whose mineral composition and chemistry match the meteorite, using observations from NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter. Its precise birthplace remains unknown.

The rock’s journey to Earth began when an asteroid or another space object struck Mars with enough force to blast material off the surface and into space. The fragment traveled through the solar system until its trajectory brought it to Earth, where it entered the atmosphere and survived the descent to the ground. Its not known exaclty when Teghaza 001 landed in the Sahara.

Finding a Martian meteorite is unusual. Only about 435 meteorites from Mars have been identified on Earth, and most are much younger than Teghaza 001. Scientists can establish their Martian origin by comparing their chemical and isotopic signatures with measurements made by spacecraft and rovers exploring the planet.

A rare record of ancient water

What makes this meteorite special is its age, minerals it contains, and what those mineerals tell us about Mars' history.

Teghaza 001 is among the oldest Martian meteorites recovered. Its minerals reveal how the Martian crust formed from cooling magma and was subsequently altered by water moving through the subsurface. That evidence is important because scientists are still working to understand how much water Mars once had, how long it persisted and what happened as the planet evolved into today’s cold, dry world.

Specialized isotope measurements of tiny zircon crystals allowed researchers to reconstruct the rock's history. Their findings indicate that water altered the rock around 4.1 billion years ago, meaning the rock itself formed even earlier.

The discovery adds to evidence that ancient Mars had conditions very different from those found on the planet today. Other spacecraft observations have revealed dried river channels, ancient lake deposits and minerals that form in the presence of water. A meteorite offers a complementary source of evidence because scientists can examine its minerals in detail using laboratory instruments.

Lee Saper, a co-author of the study who is now a scientist at NASA’s Ames Research Center, said the rock records interactions between water and minerals and may preserve clues about the Martian atmosphere as the planet was losing water.

Researchers describe the study as an initial examination of Teghaza 001, with more work needed to understand its formation and alteration. As scientists continue to investigate the meteorite, this small piece of Mars could help illuminate a period of planetary history that began billions of years before humans looked toward the Red Planet.

You can get a hands-on look at another piece of Mars at the North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences on the third floor of the Nature Research Center Postcards from Space exhibit.
